summary: Offers simple guidelines for gaining prominence and influence in standards organizations. It is advice for participants rather than a technical specification. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a guide to being a helpful, respected member of a club that writes rules for the internet: show up, be useful, and be clear.

subtitle: Simple guidelines for gaining prominence and influence in standards organizations

tldr.problem: Many people join standards organizations but struggle to gain visibility and influence among established members and leaders.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides practical guidelines: show up consistently, sit up front, build relationships through meals and mentoring, volunteer for tasks, learn the organization's culture, and speak strategically rather than on every issue.
tldr.outcome: Following these guidelines helps newcomers become noticed, respected, and eventually influential in standards bodies without requiring exceptional skills or aggressive behavior.

facts.label: Minimum attendance
facts.value: Rare absences; do not miss most events

facts.label: Seating strategy for meetings
facts.value: Front rows for visibility, or back for mobility

today: RFC 4144 is an Informational RFC published in September 2005 and remains a useful guide for newcomers to the IETF and other standards organizations. The advice reflects enduring principles of organizational culture and human dynamics.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC offers practical advice for gaining prominence and influence in standards organizations, especially the IETF. The author notes that while newcomers often perceive an inner clique controlling things, this is normal in all human organizations. The key is that following simple guidelines can accelerate how quickly you become known and respected. It takes moderate effort and normal communication skills, not exceptional talent.
sections.eli5: Every group seems to have people who run things, but you can become one of them by being smart about how you participate.

sections.title: Showing Up and Being Visible
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that eighty percent of success is simply showing up. If you are absent, you cannot have prominence or influence. Attendance is critical across all venues: email, video conferences, and especially in-person meetings. You do not need perfect attendance, but your absences should be rare and only when events are less important.

Sitting up front in meetings also matters. For small meetings under twenty people it makes little difference, but for larger meetings, sit near the front where you will be noticed. Do not be afraid of the first row. As you gain experience, you may sit with groups, but prominent people either sit near the front or way at the back where they can move around and talk to people.
sections.eli5: Show up to meetings and sit where people can see you. It is that simple.

sections.title: Building Relationships
sections.content:
All meetings include meals and refreshments. Use these opportunities strategically. If there is a catered meal, try sitting with different groups to understand various viewpoints, or sit with experienced people if they seem welcoming. For the social events common at multi-day meetings, attend and use them to have pleasant conversations with high-level officials, but do not expect detailed technical discussions.

Develop friends and mentors by introducing yourself and being friendly. Seek out people who are knowledgeable and well-regarded within the organization, not just the first people you meet. Volunteer to do necessary drudgery like taking notes, helping draft proposals, or rewriting sections for clarity. This gets you noticed and creates goodwill, but be careful not to over-commit and fail to deliver.
sections.eli5: Eat with different people to learn how they think, find people who know the ropes, and offer to help with boring jobs nobody likes.

sections.title: Speaking and Influencing
sections.content:
Think carefully about the impression you make. If you speak to every issue, you will get a reputation as a blowhard. If you speak occasionally with solid points, people will pay much more attention. Similarly, quibbling about everything wastes goodwill and makes you look obstructionist. Instead, pick your points: consider how important an issue is to you, how strong your arguments would be, and how much opposition you might face. Only invest effort in fights you believe you can win or where the stakes are high.

Do not object to procedure just for the sake of objecting. If you repeatedly invoke little-used official rules, people will assume you are silly or obstructionist. If you do invoke the rules to override tradition on an important matter, understand that you are using a weapon of mass destruction and will almost certainly face blowback.
sections.eli5: Do not talk all the time, and do not fight about little things. When you do speak up, people will listen more.

sections.title: Learning the Organization
sections.content:
It is quite important to know the traditions of an organization: how things actually get done, what rules are ignored, how rules are interpreted, and which rules are rigorously enforced. Official procedures matter less than understanding actual practice. The probability that groups actually operate by officially adopted rules in detail is low unless the organization is very informal.

Technical and communications skills are helpful but not essential. You need to understand the technical aspects so you cannot be easily fooled. If you are very strong technically, you can contribute substantially. Strong communication skills help too, though if the organization's dominant language is not your native language, put in time to become fluent. Acronyms and special terms are standard in technical efforts. Learn them in advance, or ask about them as soon as you encounter them. Other newcomers will be grateful that you asked.
sections.eli5: Learn how your group really works, not just the rules written down. Ask about confusing words when you hear them.
